title: Emergency Procedures
description: Key concepts from AIM Chapter 6 covering emergency procedures, distress communications, ELTs, and survival

cards.back:
14 CFR 91.3: Pilot-in-command is:
• Directly responsible for aircraft operation
• Final authority as to aircraft operation

In EMERGENCY:
• May deviate from ANY rule to meet emergency
• Must notify ATC ASAP if deviated from clearance
• May be required to submit written report

DISTRESS:
• Immediate danger to life or property
• Requires immediate assistance
• Use MAYDAY

URGENCY:
• Concerns safety of aircraft
• Does NOT require immediate assistance
• Use PAN-PAN

When in doubt - DECLARE!

7700: EMERGENCY
• '77 - going to heaven'

7600: COMMUNICATION FAILURE
• '76 - need to fix (radio)'

7500: HIJACK
• '75 - taken alive'

Squawk 7700 even if no radar contact - triggers alerts!

1. MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY
2. (Facility name) if able
3. Aircraft callsign
4. Type of aircraft
5. Nature of emergency
6. Intentions/request
7. Present position and altitude
8. Fuel remaining (hours:minutes)
9. Souls on board
10. Any other useful information

121.5 MHz: International emergency
• VHF guard frequency
• Most ATC and aircraft monitor
• ELTs transmit on this

243.0 MHz: Military emergency
• UHF guard frequency

Use ANY frequency you're on - ATC will coordinate!

406 MHz ELT (preferred):
• Satellite monitored (Cospas-Sarsat)
• Digital encoding with owner data
• GPS position capability
• Must register with NOAA
• Includes 121.5 MHz homing signal

121.5/243.0 MHz (legacy):
• NO longer satellite monitored (since 2009)
• Relies on overflying aircraft/ATC

When: Only during first 5 minutes after each hour

How:
• Test duration: 3 audible sweeps maximum
• Tune to 121.5 MHz to verify

False activations:
• Check after hard landings
• Notify ATC immediately if inadvertent activation

SAR begins when:
• Information suggests aircraft is missing
• 30+ min overdue AND cannot contact
• ELT signal received

Without flight plan: SAR may not begin until reported missing by family/friends!

ALWAYS file and close flight plans!

Steady GREEN: Cleared to land
Flashing GREEN: Return for landing
Steady RED: Give way, continue circling
Flashing RED: Airport unsafe, don't land
Alternating RED/GREEN: Extreme caution
Flashing WHITE: Not used in flight

Acknowledge: Rock wings (day), flash lights (night)

Steady GREEN: Cleared for takeoff
Flashing GREEN: Cleared to taxi
Steady RED: STOP
Flashing RED: Taxi clear of runway in use
Flashing WHITE: Return to starting point
Alternating RED/GREEN: Extreme caution

Acknowledge: Move ailerons (day), flash lights (night)

If VFR pilot inadvertently enters IMC:
1. Maintain aircraft control
2. Reverse course to VFR if possible
3. If not possible - declare DISTRESS
4. State: 'I am not instrument rated'
5. Request radar vectors to VFR
6. Follow ATC instructions precisely
7. Trust instruments, not senses!

Squawk: 7600
Route: A-V-E-F (Assigned, Vectored, Expected, Filed)
Altitude: HIGHEST of assigned, expected, or MEA

Approach: Begin at expected time OR if no expect time, upon arrival at fix

Always report loss of comm if able via phone after landing

Service provided by some ATC facilities:
• Determines aircraft bearing from radio transmission
• Provides heading to airport

To use:
• Contact ATC, state emergency
• Request DF steer
• Key mic as directed for signal
• Follow heading instructions

SAR may provide:
• Visual/electronic contact with distressed aircraft
• In-flight assistance
• Escort to safe landing
• Immediate SAR if ditching/crash occurs

Pilot may refuse escort service
Escort continues to nearest adequate airport

MINIMUM FUEL:
• Advisory - cannot accept undue delay
• NOT an emergency declaration
• ATC informed of priority need

FUEL EMERGENCY:
• Declare when fuel CRITICAL
• State 'DECLARING EMERGENCY'
• Will receive priority handling

Don't wait until it's too late!

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS:
1. Pitch for best glide speed
2. Pick landing spot (usually ahead)
3. Attempt restart if time/altitude
4. Secure engine (mixture, fuel, mags)
5. Declare emergency if able
6. Unlatch doors before touchdown
7. Master OFF before touchdown

Aviate, Navigate, Communicate!

POH procedures typically include:
1. Mixture - CUTOFF
2. Fuel selector - OFF
3. Fuel pump - OFF
4. Master - OFF (if fire persists)
5. Cabin heat/air - OFF
6. Airspeed - increase to extinguish
7. Forced landing - ASAP

DECLARE EMERGENCY!

POH procedures typically:
1. Master - OFF
2. Avionics - OFF
3. Cabin heat/air - OFF
4. Fire extinguisher - use if available
5. Ventilate cabin
6. If fire out, turn master ON
7. Turn on essential equipment one at a time
8. Land as soon as practical

Automated alert to controllers:
• Warns of terrain/obstacle proximity
• Mode C aircraft under ATC control

Provided for:
• All IFR flights
• VFR flights - BY REQUEST

Phrase: 'Request MSAW monitoring'

Limitations: May not work near borders

Air Force Rescue Coordination Center:
• Coordinates inland US SAR
• Receives 406 ELT alerts
• Phone: 1-800-851-3051

US Coast Guard:
• Coordinates maritime SAR
• Coastal and oceanic areas

Both work with Civil Air Patrol

For flights over uninhabited areas:
• Water (1 gal/person/day)
• Food (energy bars, MREs)
• Shelter (space blanket, tarp)
• Signaling (mirror, flare, whistle)
• First aid kit
• Fire starting equipment
• Navigation (map, compass)
• Clothing appropriate to conditions

Ground-to-air signals:
• V = Require assistance
• X = Require medical
• N = No/negative
• Y = Yes/affirmative
• → = Proceeding this direction

Make signals large (at least 8 ft)
Use contrasting materials
Stay with aircraft unless rescue certain

If intercepted:
• Follow interceptor's visual signals
• Squawk 7700
• Attempt contact on 121.5 or 243.0
• Respond to signals:
 - Rock wings = Acknowledge
 - Follow me = Comply
 - Land = Follow to airport

Never make aggressive maneuvers!

Symptoms:
• Headache, dizziness, drowsiness
• Similar to hypoxia
• Odorless, colorless gas

Sources: Exhaust through cabin heater

Action:
1. Heater - OFF
2. Vents - OPEN
3. Windows - OPEN if able
4. Land as soon as practical
5. Seek medical attention

DON'THESITATE:
• If in doubt, declare
• Better safe than sorry
• No penalty for good judgment

BENEFITS:
• Priority handling
• All available resources
• Cleared path to airport
• Emergency equipment standing by

Remember: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

Before ditching:
• Declare emergency, position
• Consider USCG if over water
• Deploy survival gear
• Secure loose items
• Land parallel to swells, into wind

In water:
• Exit quickly
• Inflate life vest OUTSIDE aircraft
• Deploy raft, stay with group
• Signal for rescue

Symptoms (vary by person):
• Headache, dizziness
• Impaired judgment/euphoria
• Tingling, visual changes
• Blue fingernails (cyanosis)

Treatment:
1. Don oxygen mask/supplement
2. Descend to lower altitude
3. Land if symptoms persist

Onset: Above 10,000-12,000 ft

Causes:
• Vestibular illusions
• Lack of visual reference (IMC)
• Trust body vs instruments

Prevention:
• Trust instruments in IMC
• Avoid sudden head movements
• Maintain scan pattern

Recovery:
• Level by instruments
• Don't chase sensations
• Get to VFR or declare emergency

When emergency declared:
• Aircraft receives priority
• Other traffic moved/held
• Direct routing provided
• Runway cleared
• Emergency equipment alerted
• ARFF standing by

Never delay declaring for fear of 'getting in trouble'

After emergency deviation:
• Submit written report if requested
• 14 CFR 91.3(c)
• Within 10 days if requested

Cover in report:
• Nature of emergency
• Actions taken
• Rules deviated from
• Justification

Honest reporting protects you
